name: Trestolone (MENT)

card.summary: Trestolone (MENT): an experimental potent androgen developed for male contraception and replacement, now floated on looksmax.org as a topical 'facial remodeling' idea with no supporting data.
card.note: Never approved; the only registered trial found is a blood-pressure study in normal men, and forum facial-androgen ideas are speculative.

quick.overview:
Trestolone, also called MENT (7-alpha-methyl-19-nortestosterone), is an experimental synthetic androgen that was developed for male hormonal contraception and androgen replacement. It has not been approved as a medicine. In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing spaces it is mentioned as a very potent androgen, sometimes called ment.

The only human research located is a registered phase 1 trial of its effects on blood pressure in normal men. On looksmax.org, one thread proposes applying transdermal androgens to the jawline for facial remodeling, a speculative idea that other users challenged and that no study supports.
quick.mechanism: Grokipedia describes it as a potent androgen-receptor agonist with progestogenic activity that is not converted to DHT by 5-alpha-reductase and that suppresses gonadotropins; this is the basis for its research as a contraceptive.[1] The looksmax.org claim of local jawline binding is a forum hypothesis.[2]
quick.risks: Because it is unapproved, safety knowledge comes from small research studies, including a registered trial of its effect on blood pressure in 68 men.[3] Forum users anticipate acne, skin irritation and more facial hair from the topical idea, and one asked that any tester be someone not prone to acne or baldness.[2]

lead: Trestolone, known in research as MENT (7-alpha-methyl-19-nortestosterone), is an experimental synthetic androgen. Within physique and looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a very potent androgen that could, in principle, add muscle and fullness to the frame, and one looksmax.org thread has proposed applying it to the skin over the jaw in the hope of sharpening the jawline.[2] It has never been approved or marketed as a medicine.[5]

Its research history is medical. First described in 1963, it was revisited from about 1990 and developed by the Population Council as a candidate for male hormonal contraception and androgen replacement, typically delivered by subcutaneous implant.[5][1][8] Studies in hypogonadal men and in contraceptive trials reported that it behaves like a strong androgen that is not converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5-alpha-reductase.[5][7]

The only registered human trial located is a two-part phase 1 study of MENT and blood pressure in 68 normal men, started in 2008.[3] No study has examined trestolone for muscle appearance or for facial or jaw bone, and the forum jaw proposal is a hypothesis that other users questioned in replies.[2]

paras: Trestolone was investigated for two purposes. As a male contraceptive, it was meant to suppress luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone so that sperm production falls, while providing enough androgen to maintain male characteristics.[9][5] As an androgen replacement for hypogonadal men, it was studied in implant form to deliver continuous low doses over months.[7][9] Grokipedia says development slowed because of variability in implant release and limited funding.[1] Wikipedia notes that no development has been recorded since 2013.[5] Cochrane reviews of randomized trials of male hormonal contraception provide the broader context in which such agents were studied.[14]

Physique-oriented users describe trestolone as a very potent anabolic androgen, an impression that follows from preclinical findings that it is far more potent than testosterone at supporting muscle in animals.[5] For appearance purposes the most specific proposal appears on looksmax.org, where a thread titled as an aggressive androgenic facial remodeling stack suggests applying transdermal DHT, trenbolone and MENT together with an IGF-1 analogue to the jaw. The poster argued that topical androgens would be absorbed locally and bind receptors in the jawline, drawing on published reports of topical DHT used for micropenis in partial androgen insensitivity; he acknowledged likely acne, irritation, more facial hair and systemic absorption.[2] One reply asked for a volunteer who is not prone to acne or balding; another said that DHT acts locally but has no noticeable effect on bone, and that slowing bone breakdown is not the same as bone growth.[2] A second thread titled 'Enjoy the ment' also exists, with no content usable here.[4]

A registered phase 1 trial (NCT00812630), begun in December 2008 and completed, examined the effect of MENT on blood pressure in normal men, first in an open-label pilot and then in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled part with 68 participants.[3]

A 24-week randomized trial gave MENT acetate implants (one or two, each releasing roughly 400 micrograms per day) to 16 hypogonadal men and examined tissue selectivity, including haemoglobin and hematocrit; its title reports evidence that the androgen acts selectively across tissues, with the prostate spared because MENT resists 5-alpha-reduction.[7] A separate randomized trial tested MENT implants as a long-acting male contraceptive, measuring antispermatogenic effect using ethylene vinyl acetate implants.[8] Earlier pharmacokinetic work studied subdermal implants in healthy men and compared kinetics in men and cynomolgus monkeys.[10][11] A 1993 review described MENT as an optimal androgen candidate for contraception because it is considerably more potent than testosterone and, lacking 5-alpha-reduction, should not hyperstimulate the prostate at doses that maintain muscle mass.[6]
No study has examined trestolone for physique or facial appearance.

Published adverse-effect information is limited. Wikipedia lists reduced libido and erectile function and lower bone mineral density among reported effects in treated men, the latter attributed to low estrogen when natural testosterone production is suppressed.[5] Because trestolone suppresses gonadotropins, fertility falls while it is used and, per Wikipedia, recovers quickly after discontinuation.[5] The forum poster anticipated acne, irritation and facial hair from topical use.[2] Under Grokipedia's account, mood effects are also possible.[1]

Wikipedia dates the first description of trestolone to 1963 and says it was not studied again until 1990; by 1993 it was being developed by the Population Council, a non-profit reproductive health organization, for male hormonal contraception and androgen replacement.[5] A 1993 review in Annals of Medicine presented it as a suitable androgen for year-long delivery by subdermal implant.[6]

Trials around 2003 tested implants in hypogonadal men and as a contraceptive, and Wikipedia reports that no further development appears to have occurred since 2013.[7][8][5] Wikipedia's article on male contraceptives places MENT among 1990s and early-2000s implant research that did not lead to an approved product, while later candidates such as NES/T gel, dimethandrolone undecanoate and 11-beta-MNTDC remain in clinical development.[15] A separate injectable testosterone-progestin trial was halted in 2011 on the advice of a WHO review panel citing adverse events including mood changes and depression, although many participants reported satisfaction.[15]

Trestolone is a synthetic estrane steroid and a derivative of nandrolone (19-nortestosterone) carrying a methyl group at the 7-alpha position. Wikipedia lists related compounds including mibolerone, dimethandrolone, dimethyltrienolone and tibolone, and notes it is an intermediate in synthesising mibolerone and tibolone.[5] The 2003 delivery review describes 7-alpha-methylation and 19-nor modification as structural changes made to raise androgenic potency or alter duration compared with testosterone.[9]

Trestolone is an androgen-receptor agonist with an affinity comparable to testosterone and also has potent progestogenic activity.[5] It is not a substrate for 5-alpha-reductase, so it is not amplified in skin, hair follicles and prostate the way testosterone is, which underlies the contraceptive-research interest in prostate sparing.[5][6] It can be aromatized to a weak estrogen, 7-alpha-methylestradiol.[5][12] In monkeys, implants were reported to be about ten times as potent as testosterone for gonadotropin suppression and anabolic effects, but only about twice as potent for prostate growth.[5] Wikipedia reports relative binding affinities of about 100-125% at the androgen receptor and 50-75% at the progesterone receptor against reference ligands, and describes a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio.[5] It suppresses LH and FSH, lowering sperm production and endogenous testosterone, an effect reported to be reversible after stopping.[5] Its quick clearance is partly attributed to not binding sex hormone-binding globulin.[5]

Poor oral bioavailability and a short elimination half-life make it unsuitable for oral dosing or long-term intramuscular injection of the free compound; research used implants, patches or gels, and an acetate prodrug can be injected.[5][9][11] A 2026 study investigated its human metabolism, relevant to doping-control detection.[13]

Trestolone has no approved medical use and is not marketed by a pharmaceutical company.[5] Grokipedia says it appears in bodybuilding circles as a research compound; this wiki does not give sourcing or use guidance.[1]

timeline.event: First described by Lyster and Duncan.[5]
Research interest resumes after decades without study.[5]
Population Council develops MENT implants as a male contraceptive and androgen replacement candidate.[5][15]
Review proposes MENT as an optimal androgen for male contraception.[6]
Randomized trials report on MENT implants in hypogonadal men and as a male contraceptive.[7][8]
A phase 1 trial of MENT effects on blood pressure in normal men begins.[3]
A separate WHO-reviewed injectable testosterone-progestin male contraceptive trial is halted over adverse events, shaping the field in which MENT was studied.[15]
A study of human metabolism of trestolone for doping-control detection is published.[13]

lore.intro: Trestolone is mentioned on looksmax.org as an extremely potent androgen, with one thread proposing topical use on the jaw.[2][4]

claims.claim: Topical androgens like DHT, tren and MENT bind locally in the jawline and could remodel the face.
claims.believers: The thread starter argues that topical DHT works for penile enlargement with less systemic absorption and infers that jawline application would bind local androgen receptors.[2]
claims.experts: No published study tests topical trestolone or any androgen for facial bone remodeling in adults; the cited evidence concerns topical DHT in children with partial androgen insensitivity.[2]

claims.claim: Androgens' effect on bone preservation implies bone growth.
claims.believers: The poster pointed to papers on androgens and bone as support.[2]
claims.experts: A reply in the thread notes that preventing bone breakdown is not the same as causing growth; no trial has examined this for facial bones.[2]

claims.claim: MENT is a far more potent anabolic than testosterone.
claims.believers: Forum users describe it as very potent.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports about tenfold anabolic potency in monkeys relative to testosterone; the only registered human trial studied blood pressure, and no study has measured physique outcomes.[5][3]

chain: Proposed to build lean mass or, as a forum idea, to act on the jaw when applied locally
angle.text: Users who discuss trestolone treat it as a strong anabolic androgen that could support lean mass, and one forum thread proposes applying androgens to the jawline for facial remodeling. These are claims drawn from its pharmacology and forum reasoning; research on the compound itself has addressed contraception, replacement and blood pressure.
